page.title: Catches that drop the failure
page.body: In #5 the failure handler answered with an empty list, and in #7 the new catch around the client call returns null, so a fetch error vanishes either way. Silent fallbacks hide the fact that the fetch failed and make the failure hard to find. A future caller can tell success from a swallowed error only by guessing what an empty result means.
page.nextStep: When you write or edit a catch, decide what the caller should know: rethrow it, or record it with the context that explains what was being attempted.

composition.summary:
Catch swallows the failure

Situation: In fetch, the new catch for IOException returns null without recording the error, so a failed call looks like a missing record and the failure disappears.

Capability: The developer can check whether the code that reacts to a failure also leaves a trace: it records, reports or rethrows the exception instead of silently substituting a value.

Evidence: The change in the retry branch (acme/app, PR #7) wraps client.get(id) in a try and its catch (IOException) returns null at the end of fetch, per the NOT_MET result on the swallowed failure.

In conversation: Before the turn ends the developer states why a caught failure should be recorded or rethrown rather than turned into null, and names what fetch should do when the call fails.
